title: Ordinary WiFi Can Recognise You Through a Wall
hook: The radio waves already bouncing around your flat carry a shape — yours. Researchers turned unencrypted WiFi chatter into an image good enough to identify 197 people almost perfectly.
key_points: WiFi is microwave-band radio; your body reflects, absorbs, and delays those waves, imprinting itself on what the router receives.
Routine unencrypted signals exchanged between devices and routers were enough — no camera, no special sensor, no phone carried by the person.
From those signals the researchers reconstructed radio-based images of people and recognised them within seconds.
In tests with 197 participants, identification accuracy was near 100%, from different angles and regardless of gait.
The physics is ordinary reflection and interference; the privacy implication is that any WiFi network is a latent imaging system.
content_html: WiFi is not a special kind of signal; it is microwave-band electromagnetic radiation, obeying the same reflection and interference rules as light. Which means that when it fills a room, everything in the room leaves a mark on it. A body is mostly water, so it absorbs some of the wave, reflects some, and delays what passes around it — and that distortion arrives at the router along with the data.
extra_html: Researchers, in work reported via ScienceDaily, showed how much of a person survives in that distortion. They used the unencrypted signals routinely exchanged between WiFi devices and access points — nothing intercepted from the encrypted payload, no camera, and no connected device on the person — and reconstructed radio-based images of people from them. In tests with 197 participants, the system identified individuals with nearly 100% accuracy within seconds, from different viewing angles and independent of how each person walked. The physics here is not new, which is rather the point: the sensing capability is a side effect of how radio propagation works, so it comes free with any WiFi network. The authors frame it as a warning that ordinary networks are quietly capable of camera-free surveillance.

related.title: Electricity & Magnetism Are One Force
related.hook: Move a magnet near a wire and you make electricity; run current through a wire and you make a magnet. They're two faces of the same force.

related.title: Electric and Magnetic Fields
related.hook: How does a magnet pull a paperclip it isn't touching? Through a field — an invisible region of influence that tells other charges and magnets how to feel a force.

flashcards.prompt: What physical effect lets WiFi signals carry information about a person's body?
flashcards.back_html: A body reflects, absorbs, and delays the radio waves passing through a room, so the signal arriving at the router is altered in a person-specific way.

flashcards.prompt: What made the WiFi identification result unsettling from a privacy standpoint?

choices.text: It used routine unencrypted router traffic, with no camera and no device carried by the person
It required breaking the network's WPA encryption first
It only worked if the person was wearing a WiFi-enabled wearable

flashcards.explanation_html: The signals were the ordinary unencrypted exchanges between devices and routers, meaning existing networks can act as surveillance sensors without any added hardware.

flashcards.prompt: How accurate was the system, and on how many people?
flashcards.back_html: Near 100% identification across 197 participants — holding up from different angles and regardless of how each person walked.
